197.title: Who's the greatest? (Mark 9:30–37)
197.hook: they argue about rank; he puts a child in the middle
197.carry: last of all, servant of all
197.howItsDone: Churches of many traditions have deacons, a word from the Greek for servant, who care for the poor and help at worship, and some Christians point to this passage when talking about leadership as service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a father at the foot of the mountain prayed with belief and doubt in one breath. Your line was bring the half you have.

What were you arguing about back there? Ask that after a long car ride with kids in the back seat, and you get silence. Everyone suddenly fascinated by the window. That's this scene. Jesus is passing quietly through Galilee, and for the second time he tells his friends he'll be handed over and killed, and rise the third day. They don't understand, and they're afraid to ask. Then, in the house in Capernaum, he asks what they were arguing about on the road. Mark tells us, in the King James Bible: "But they held their peace: for by the way they had disputed among themselves, who should be the greatest."
screen: `A SECOND WARNING ON THE ROAD.` → `WHAT WERE YOU ARGUING ABOUT?` → `SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Notice the timing. He has just told them he's going to suffer and die, and they spend the walk arguing about who's number one. Mark doesn't soften it. Jesus doesn't shout, either. He sits down, calls the twelve over, and says: "If any man desire to be first, the same shall be last of all, and servant of all." The Greek word for servant is diakonos, the one who waits on tables. It's where the church later got the word deacon. The ladder turns upside down: the greatest is the one bringing the plates. Then he shows them. He takes a child, stands the child in the middle of the circle of grown men, and takes the child up in his arms. Whoever welcomes one little child like this in my name, he says, welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me. A small child can do nothing for anyone's rank. Welcoming one wins you nothing. That seems to be the point. Churches still meet this in ordinary ways: who gets the seat at the front, who serves the coffee, who is noticed. The argument on the road is very old, and very ordinary. And his answer is sitting in the middle of the room, in his arms.

segments.voice: Think of someone younger than you whom you'll see today: a child, a grandchild, a student, a new person at work, the youngest in the family chat. What would serving them look like: listening to the whole long story, making them something, asking their opinion and meaning it? Choose one thing, and if you pray, hold them before God.
Diakonos, the Greek word for servant, the one who waits on tables. The argument on the road. His answer: the last of all, the servant of all, and a child in the middle.

198.title: Not one of us (Mark 9:38–41)
198.hook: whoever is not against us is for us
198.howItsDone: Some churches take part in a yearly Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, when Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant congregations pray together or visit one another.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was diakonos, the one who waits on tables, and he stood a child in the middle. Your line was last of all, servant of all.

The right jersey. The right school. The group chat you were or weren't added to. Groups have unofficial rules about who's in. Now, just after the lesson about the child, John speaks up. Mark has told us Jesus nicknamed him and his brother the sons of thunder. He seems pleased with his news. In the King James Bible: "Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name, and he followeth not us: and we forbad him, because he followeth not us." A stranger, doing good in the name of Jesus, and they shut him down. Listen to the reason, twice over. Not: he doesn't follow you. He doesn't follow us.
screen: `WHO'S IN THE GROUP?` → `A STRANGER, USING THE NAME.` → `HE FOLLOWETH NOT US.`

segments.voice: Jesus answers in three short words: "Forbid him not." Nobody who does a mighty work in my name, he says, can turn around the next moment and speak evil of me. Then the line: "For he that is not against us is on our part." The circle is wider than John drew it. And he sets the bar lower still: whoever gives you a cup of water to drink in my name, because you belong to Christ, will not lose their reward. A cup of water. The Hebrew Bible has a scene like this. In the book of Numbers, two men named Eldad and Medad start prophesying in the camp without having been at the official gathering, and young Joshua begs Moses to stop them. Moses says, in effect: I wish all the Lord's people were prophets. To be fair, the Gospels also keep a saying that sounds like the opposite. In Matthew, Jesus says whoever is not with me is against me. Christians keep both. Some read Matthew's as about where a person stands toward Jesus himself, and today's as about how his followers treat people outside their own circle. Churches today differ, and argue about real things. Some also set aside a yearly week to pray for Christian unity, side by side. The disciples asked who's with us. His answer was who's for us.

199.title: Salt (Mark 9:42–50)
199.hook: have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another
199.howItsDone: Christians often speak of being "the salt of the earth" and read Mark 9:50 as a call to keep their faith lively and to make peace within the church; in some congregations people share the peace, a greeting or handshake, during worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John tried to stop a stranger, and heard forbid him not. Your line was not against us, for us.

Still in the same house, with the friends who argued about rank, Jesus says some of the hardest-sounding things in Mark. Whoever trips up one of these little ones who believe, better for them to have a millstone hung around their neck and be thrown into the sea. If your hand makes you stumble, cut it off. If your foot, cut it off. If your eye, pluck it out. Better to enter life missing a part than, in the King James words, to be cast into hell fire. Church tradition reads them as deliberate exaggeration, not instructions. Then, right at the end, the tone changes, and he talks about something on every kitchen table.
screen: `A MILLSTONE AND THE SEA.` → `CUT IT OFF.` → `SOMETHING ON EVERY TABLE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Salt is good: but if the salt have lost his saltness, wherewith will ye season it? Have salt in yourselves, and have peace one with another." Salt was precious. Before refrigerators, it kept fish and meat from rotting, and it gave taste. In the Hebrew Bible, offerings were seasoned with salt, and there's a phrase, a covenant of salt, for a promise meant to last. Can salt really lose its saltness? Pure salt can't. Some readers suggest the salt people used then was mixed with other minerals, so damp could wash the true salt out and leave white stuff that tasted of nothing. Just before comes a line nobody is sure about: "every one shall be salted with fire." Mark doesn't explain it; readers still puzzle. The ending is clear: salt in yourselves, and peace with one another. He's talking to the men who argued about rank and shut out the stranger. One way to hear it: keep your taste, your bite. Just don't turn the bite on each other. That closes this stretch of Mark, the one that kept asking who is this. Washed hands and what comes out of the heart. Crumbs for a mother's daughter. Be opened. Seven baskets. Hard hearts in a boat. Men like trees. You are the Christ. Take up your cross. Listen to him. Help my unbelief. Who's the greatest. Not one of us. And salt. Tomorrow the road turns south, toward Jerusalem.
screen: `SALT KEPT THINGS AND GAVE TASTE.` · `SALT THAT LOSES ITS SALTNESS.` · `SALTED WITH FIRE: NOBODY'S SURE.` · `SALT IN YOU, PEACE WITH EACH OTHER.` · then, large: `HAVE SALT IN YOURSELVES, AND HAVE PEACE ONE WITH ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you're a little crossways with right now, nothing huge: a sharp text, a cold week, a silence that went on too long. Keep your salt, you don't have to pretend you were wrong about everything, but ask what one step toward peace would look like: a message, a kind word, letting it go. If you pray, bring them to God by name.
Salt. It keeps things and gives them taste. Have salt in yourselves, he says, and have peace one with another.
Your line: salt, and peace. Keep your bite, and keep the peace. Day one hundred ninety-nine, done.

200.title: Marriage (Mark 10:1–12)
200.hook: asked about divorce, he points back to creation; churches today apply this in differing ways
200.howItsDone: Many Christian wedding services echo Mark 10:9, that what God has joined no one should put asunder, and many churches pray for married couples during worship; churches differ on divorce and remarriage, from the Catholic Church's annulment process to the Orthodox and many Protestant churches' provisions for remarriage.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was salt; your line, salt, and peace. Now a new stretch of Mark: the road to Jerusalem.

Chapter ten, and the road turns south. Jesus leaves Galilee for Judea and the land beyond the Jordan, and crowds gather again. Some Pharisees come with a question, and Mark tells us it's a test. Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife? The Law of Moses allowed a man to write his wife a certificate of divorce and send her away, and teachers disagreed sharply over what reasons were good enough. Whatever Jesus says, someone will be unhappy. Almost everyone listening knows a marriage that held, and one that broke. He goes not to the rules, but back to the beginning.
screen: `THE ROAD TURNS SOUTH.` → `IS IT LAWFUL?` → `BACK TO THE BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: What did Moses command, he asks. Moses allowed a certificate of divorce, they say. Jesus says Moses wrote that because of the hardness of your hearts. It's a different Greek word from the hard hearts in the boat on day one ninety-one, but the same picture: a heart gone stiff. Then he reaches past Moses to Genesis: from the beginning God made them male and female, and a man shall leave his father and mother, and the two shall be one flesh. Then the line still heard at weddings, in the King James Bible: "What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder." Asunder means apart. Later, in the house, he goes further with the disciples: whoever divorces and marries another commits adultery. Mark also includes a wife divorcing her husband, which fit Roman law more than the Jewish custom of the day. And divorce then often meant a woman sent away with a piece of paper, and often nothing to live on. Many readers hear in his words a protection for the one most likely to be discarded. Churches apply this differently, and each takes it seriously. The Catholic Church teaches that a valid sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved, and it can declare that a marriage was never valid, an annulment. Orthodox churches hold marriage as lifelong, yet may allow a second marriage with a service of repentance. Many Protestant churches allow divorce in some circumstances, such as adultery or abandonment, reading this alongside Matthew and Paul. What they share is the starting point Jesus chose: not the loophole, but the beginning.
screen: `WHAT DID MOSES COMMAND?` · `FOR THE HARDNESS OF YOUR HEART.` · `FROM THE BEGINNING: ONE FLESH.` · `CHURCHES APPLY IT DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `WHAT THEREFORE GOD HATH JOINED TOGETHER, LET NOT MAN PUT ASUNDER.`

segments.voice: Hold one marriage in your mind: your own, your parents', a friend's, a couple just starting, one that's struggling right now, or even one that ended, and the people still living with that. Picture them both kindly: what do they need? Patience, time together, rest. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, wish them well, slowly and on purpose.
Marriage. Asked about divorce, Jesus answers with the beginning: two becoming one flesh, joined by God.
Your line: what god joined. Day two hundred, and still walking together.

201.title: Let the children come (Mark 10:13–16)
201.hook: the disciples shoo away children, and he's indignant
201.howItsDone: Some churches that baptize infants read this passage at baptisms, and some churches that baptize believers read it at services where parents present a baby for dedication and blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hard question about divorce, answered from the beginning. Your line was what god joined.

A waiting room. A toddler, a parent, and a person at the desk giving that look: keep the little one quiet and out of the way. Now the disciples wear that look. Parents are bringing their young children to Jesus, just so he'll touch them, and the disciples rebuke them and send them off. He's busy. He's important. There's serious talk going on about divorce and the Law. Take the kids home. Mark tells us how Jesus took it: when he saw it, he was much displeased. Not with the parents. Not with the children. With his friends.
screen: `PARENTS BRING THEIR LITTLE ONES.` → `THE DISCIPLES SEND THEM OFF.` → `HE'S MUCH DISPLEASED.`

segments.voice: Much displeased is the King James phrase. The Greek word is stronger: indignant. Matthew and Luke tell this story too, and both leave that part out. Mark keeps it. Then the words: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God." Suffer, in King James English, meant allow. Let them come. Then the line that turns it into a lesson for the grown-ups: whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a little child will not enter it. How does a little child receive something? Watch a toddler handed a cookie. No negotiating, no asking what's the catch, no working out whether they've earned it. Hands open, and it's theirs. One way Christians hear the saying: the kingdom isn't a prize for the deserving, but a gift, for people willing to receive one. Mark ends the scene with three verbs: he took them up in his arms, put his hands on them, and blessed them. Not a pat on the head from a distance. Churches read this passage in different settings. Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and Reformed churches baptize infants, and some read this passage at a baptism. Baptist and other churches baptize those old enough to profess faith, and some read it when parents bring a baby to be dedicated and blessed. Either way, the children end up in his arms.
screen: `ONLY MARK KEEPS HIS INDIGNATION.` · `SUFFER MEANS ALLOW.` · `RECEIVE IT LIKE A CHILD.` · `ARMS, HANDS, BLESSING.` · then, large: `FOR OF SUCH IS THE KINGDOM OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Notice one thing you've been given today that you didn't earn: the breath you're taking right now, sunlight, a message from someone, your own hands. Don't analyze it or ask whether you deserve it; just take it, the way a toddler takes a cookie, with open hands. If you pray, you can simply say thank you, like a child would.
Indignant, the strong word behind Jesus's anger when the disciples turned the children away. His lesson: receive the kingdom as a child receives a gift.
Your line: like a child. A gift is for receiving. Rest easy tonight.

202.title: The rich young man (Mark 10:17–22)
202.hook: Jesus looked at him and loved him, then asked for everything
202.howItsDone: Some Christians, especially in monastic orders, take vows of poverty inspired by this story; others read it as a call to examine what holds them back, and to give generously to the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was indignant: the disciples shooed the children away, and he took them in his arms. Your line was like a child.

A man comes running up as Jesus sets out on the road again. He kneels in the road and asks a question as big as they come: "Good Master, what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?" Jesus pushes back on the compliment first: why call me good? No one is good but God alone. Then: you know the commandments. Don't commit adultery, don't kill, don't steal, don't bear false witness, don't defraud, honor your father and mother. And the man says, I've kept all these since I was young. Nothing in Mark suggests he's boasting. And still, he ran.
screen: `A MAN COMES RUNNING.` → `WHAT SHALL I DO?` → `I'VE KEPT THEM ALL.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Then Jesus beholding him loved him, and said unto him, One thing thou lackest: go thy way, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, take up the cross, and follow me." Look at the order. He looks at him. He loves him. Only then does he ask the hardest thing. Mark is the only gospel that says Jesus loved him; Matthew and Luke tell the story and leave it out. And Mark never says he was young. Matthew calls him a young man, and Luke calls him a ruler. Our title stitches the Gospels together. Then the line that closes the scene: "And he was sad at that saying, and went away grieved: for he had great possessions." He doesn't argue or sneer. He just can't do it, and walks away sad. And Jesus lets him go. What happened to him after? The Gospels are silent. Christians read the command in more than one way. Some have taken it literally: the early monk Anthony of Egypt, the story goes, heard this read in church and gave away his family's land. Others read it as aimed at this one man, and at whatever holds a person back from following. Either way, Mark puts the love first: the hard word comes after the long look, from someone who, the text says, loved him.

segments.voice: Think of someone you'd like to tell something to, advice, a correction, a hard truth, and before any of that, just look at them in your mind: their face, what they're carrying, what they're good at. Stay there a moment, and let some warmth toward them come, if it will; if you pray, ask to see them the way Jesus looked at the man. Only then, if you still need to, decide what you'd say.

Your line: he loved him. He let the man walk away, still loved. That's day two hundred two.

203.title: A camel and a needle (Mark 10:23–31)
203.hook: with people it's impossible, but not with God
203.howItsDone: Christians often turn to this passage when talking about money and generosity; some give a regular share of their income to church and charity, and some traditions encourage giving away something valued, especially in Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was agapao: Jesus looked at a good man and loved him, and the man walked away sad. Your line was he loved him.

The man with great possessions is still walking away down the road, and Jesus watches him go. Then he looks around at his friends. In the King James Bible: "How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!" The disciples, Mark says, were astonished at his words. He says it again, more gently, calling them children. Then he reaches for a picture that's almost absurd. A huge, lumbering animal. A hole you can barely thread. The kind of thing you'd say to make someone laugh out loud, and then go very quiet.
screen: `HE WATCHES THE MAN GO.` → `HOW HARDLY SHALL THEY.` → `A CAMEL, A NEEDLE.`

segments.voice: "It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God." People have tried hard to make this easier. You may have heard of a small gate in Jerusalem's wall called the Eye of the Needle, where a camel had to kneel and squeeze through. It's a lovely sermon illustration, but Mark says nothing about a gate. Others have wondered whether camel should be rope. But the text says camel, and the disciples don't hear a tight squeeze. They hear impossible. They were astonished out of measure, Mark says: then who can be saved? Jesus looks at them: "With men it is impossible, but not with God: for with God all things are possible." In the story, the camel doesn't get through by trying harder. It's something only God can do. Peter blurts out: we've left everything to follow you. And Jesus promises that nobody who has left home and family for his sake will miss out; they'll receive a hundred times over, homes and brothers and sisters and mothers, now. Only Mark adds two words: with persecutions. Then: many that are first shall be last, and the last first. Look back at the week. Who's the greatest? Not one of us. Salt. Marriage. Let the children come. A rich man who walked away. And a camel. Again and again, the same upside-down shape: the last first, the child in the middle, the impossible possible.

segments.voice: Look around in your mind at the things you own, not the junk drawer, something you'd actually miss: a good jacket, a book you love, money set aside for a treat. Pick one, think of someone who'd be glad of it, and notice whether anything in you tightens; if it does, that's the camel at the needle. If you pray, you can ask for help to open your hand.
Impossible. What the disciples heard when Jesus pictured a camel squeezing through a needle's eye: with men it is impossible, but not with God.
Your line: all things are possible. Not by trying harder. That's the week, wrapped up.

fork.reveal: "With men it is impossible, but not with God: for with God all things are possible." not a smaller camel: something only God can do.

original.note: Greek: camel, the word in Mark 10:25.

trapdoor: what you thought: there was a narrow gate camels could squeeze through.
what it means: it's impossible for people, on purpose; only God makes it possible.
what a scholar hears: the text says camel, not gate or rope, and only Mark adds with persecutions to the hundredfold.
